title: 22. Interview: Containers
summary: Interview Q&A for Containers — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Containers interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine, and why does it matter?
**Answer:** A virtual machine virtualizes the hardware: the hypervisor presents a fake CPU, NIC, and disk to each guest, and each guest runs its own full kernel, init system, and user space. A container virtualizes the operating system: multiple containers share a single host kernel but each sees its own process tree, filesystem, and network via Linux namespaces, with resource limits enforced by cgroups. The differences matter operationally. VMs boot in 30–60 seconds (kernel init) versus containers in 50–500ms (process fork). VMs are gigabytes in size (full OS) versus containers in megabytes (just the app and its libs). VMs provide strong isolation (a kernel exploit in one VM does not affect others) versus containers with weaker isolation (a kernel exploit can escape to the host). VMs run any OS on any host (Windows on Linux via virtualization) versus containers requiring kernel compatibility (Linux containers need a Linux kernel). The practical consequence: containers won for stateless microservices (density, fast startup, portability) while VMs persist for stateful workloads, security-sensitive multi-tenancy, and cross-OS scenarios. AWS Firecracker (used by Lambda and Fargate) is a hybrid — a ultra-lightweight VM with container-like startup time, used precisely because VM isolation matters for multi-tenant security.

**Visual:**
```
VM:          hypervisor -> [kernel + OS + app]  per guest
             boot 30-60s, GB-sized, strong isolation
Container:   host kernel -> [namespace + app + libs]  per container
             boot <500ms, MB-sized, weaker isolation

Use VM for:        stateful, security-sensitive, cross-OS
Use container for: stateless microservices, fast scaling, portability
```

### Q2. Explain container image layers and why they matter for builds, distribution, and storage.
**Answer:** A container image is a stack of read-only layers, each representing one instruction in the Dockerfile. Each layer is content-addressed by the SHA of its content plus its parent layer's SHA, so identical layers across images have identical digests. The matters in three ways. For builds: a code change invalidates only the layers above the change — if you change `COPY app.py` but not `RUN apt install`, the apt layer is cached and skipped, making rebuilds seconds instead of minutes. For distribution: when a host pulls an image, the registry serves each layer by digest, and the host caches layers locally — the second pull of any image sharing layers with the first is nearly instant. For storage: the registry stores each unique layer once, so 1000 images all using `ubuntu:22.04` as a base share a single 80MB layer on disk. Without layering, every image would be a full disk image (gigabytes), distribution would be prohibitively expensive, and builds would never cache. The layering model is the unsung hero of the container ecosystem and the reason Docker Hub can serve millions of pulls per day economically.

**Visual:**
```
Image myapp:v1:
  layer 1: ubuntu:22.04        (80MB)  <-- shared across thousands of images
  layer 2: apt install python3 (60MB)  <-- shared across python images
  layer 3: COPY app.py          (2MB)  <-- unique to this image
  layer 4: CMD /app/start.sh    (0MB)

Build:   change app.py -> only layer 3 rebuilt, 1-2 seconds
Pull:    layer 1, 2 already cached -> only layer 3, 4 transferred
Storage: layer 1 stored once in registry, used by thousands of images
```

### Q3. What are Linux namespaces and cgroups, and how do they enable container isolation?
**Answer:** Namespaces and cgroups are the two Linux kernel features that make containers possible. Namespaces provide isolation: they give a process a view of system resources that appears to be its own. The pid namespace gives the process its own process IDs (it sees itself as PID 1). The net namespace gives it its own network interfaces, routing table, and port space. The mnt namespace gives it its own filesystem mount tree. The user namespace lets it have its own UID mapping (root inside the container is non-root outside). The uts namespace gives it its own hostname. Together these make the process believe it has its own system. Cgroups provide resource limits: they let you cap CPU, memory, block I/O, and network bandwidth for a group of processes. A container with `--cpus=1 --memory=512m` is a cgroup with those limits. Docker, containerd, and CRI-O all assemble namespaces and cgroups into a "container" abstraction via the `runc` OCI runtime, which calls the kernel syscalls (`clone`, `unshare`, `setns`) to set them up. Without namespaces, a container process would see all host processes and could interfere with them. Without cgroups, a container could consume all host CPU and RAM. Both are essential.

**Visual:**
```
Namespaces (isolation):
  pid  -> process sees only its own children
  net  -> own interfaces, ports, routing
  mnt  -> own filesystem mount tree
  user -> UID mapping (root inside != root outside)
  uts  -> own hostname

Cgroups (limits):
  cpu  -> max cores
  mem  -> max RAM
  blkio-> max disk I/O
  net  -> max bandwidth

runc: assembles namespaces + cgroups -> "container"
```

### Q4. What is the OCI (Open Container Initiative), and why did it matter for the ecosystem?
**Answer:** The OCI is a Linux Foundation project, formed in 2015 under the Docker-led governance, that defines open standards for container formats and runtimes. It has two specifications. The OCI Image Spec defines the on-disk format of a container image (manifest, config, layers) so any tool can build images consumable by any runtime. The OCI Runtime Spec defines the on-disk format of a "container bundle" (rootfs + config.json) and the lifecycle operations (create, start, kill, delete) that a runtime must implement. The reference runtime implementation is `runc`, which Docker, containerd, and CRI-O all use under the hood. Before OCI, the container ecosystem was Balkanized: Docker images only worked with Docker, rkt images only worked with rkt, and customers were locked in. After OCI, any image works with any runtime, registries are interchangeable, and customers can swap components without rewriting pipelines. The practical effect: Docker the company's fortunes declined (they could not maintain lock-in) but Docker the technology won completely. Today every major cloud, every orchestrator, and every registry supports OCI, and the container ecosystem is the most standardized part of cloud infrastructure.

**Visual:**
```
Before OCI (2015):
  Docker images -> Docker only
  rkt images    -> rkt only
  AppC spec     -> incompatible with Docker
  -> vendor lock-in, ecosystem fractured

After OCI:
  OCI Image Spec  -> any tool builds, any registry stores
  OCI Runtime Spec-> any runtime runs (runc, kata, gVisor)
  Docker, containerd, CRI-O all use runc underneath
  -> standardization, interchangeability, no lock-in
```

### Q5. Why is container orchestration necessary, and what problem does Kubernetes solve?
**Answer:** A single container is trivial — `docker run` and you are done. A production fleet of thousands of containers across hundreds of hosts is intractable without an orchestrator. The problems an orchestrator solves: scheduling (which host should run which container, based on resource requests, affinity rules, and host health), lifecycle (start, stop, restart on failure, roll out new versions, roll back on error), scaling (add or remove container instances based on load), networking (give each container a routable IP, load-balance across instances, enforce network policies), storage (attach persistent volumes to stateful containers), and configuration (inject env vars, secrets, config files). Kubernetes won the orchestrator war by 2018 because it solved all of these problems with a declarative API (you specify desired state, the controller reconciles), a mature ecosystem (Helm, Istio, Argo CD), and Google's credibility (Borg was the inspiration). The trade-off is enormous complexity — a typical production Kubernetes cluster requires RBAC, CNI, CSI, ingress, service mesh, monitoring, and dedicated SREs to operate, which is why managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) and PaaS-on-Kubernetes (Render, Cloud Run) have proliferated. Netflix's Titus predates Kubernetes and remains internal; most companies now use Kubernetes rather than building their own.

**Visual:**
```
Problems orchestrator solves:
  scheduling  -> which container on which host
  lifecycle   -> start, stop, restart, roll out, roll back
  scaling     -> add/remove instances per load
  networking  -> per-container IP, load balancing, network policy
  storage     -> persistent volumes for stateful sets
  config      -> env vars, secrets, config maps

Kubernetes won because: declarative API, mature ecosystem, Google lineage
Trade-off: enormous operational complexity -> managed k8s + PaaS-on-k8s
```

### Q6. What is a "container escape," and how do platforms defend against it?
**Answer:** A container escape is a security exploit where a malicious process inside a container breaks out of its namespace isolation and accesses the host kernel or other containers. The root cause is always a kernel vulnerability or a misconfiguration: a kernel bug that lets a container process escalate privileges, a mounted Docker socket that hands the container root-equivalent host access, a `--privileged` flag that disables most isolation, or an excessive capability set (CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN) that grants dangerous operations. Famous escapes include CVE-2019-5736 (runc override) and CVE-2022-0185 (filesystem context escape). Defenses layer multiple controls. First, never run containers as root — use a non-root user inside the image. Second, drop all Linux capabilities by default and add back only what is needed. Third, never mount the Docker socket or host `/proc` into a container. Fourth, use a hardened runtime like gVisor (Google) or Kata Containers, which run each container in a lightweight VM for stronger isolation. Fifth, run security-sensitive workloads in dedicated VMs rather than shared hosts. Sixth, keep the host kernel patched — most escapes are kernel CVEs. AWS Firecracker (used by Lambda and Fargate) is the extreme case: each workload runs in a micro-VM with kernel-level isolation, accepting a small startup-time penalty for defense in depth. Multi-tenant SaaS platforms almost always run containers inside VMs for exactly this reason.

**Visual:**
```
Defenses (layered):
1. Non-root user inside image
2. Drop all capabilities, add only needed
3. Never mount Docker socket / host /proc
4. Hardened runtime: gVisor / Kata (container in VM)
5. Sensitive workloads on dedicated VMs
6. Patch host kernel aggressively (most escapes are kernel CVEs)

AWS Firecracker: each workload in micro-VM, kernel-level isolation
   -> used by Lambda/Fargate for multi-tenant security
```

### Q7. Compare Docker, containerd, and CRI-O. Why do production clusters often skip the Docker daemon?
**Answer:** Docker is the original container product: a monolithic daemon (`dockerd`) that builds images, runs containers, manages networks and volumes, and exposes a REST API. It is convenient for developers but includes components production clusters do not need (image building, plugin management, the Docker CLI). containerd is the high-level runtime extracted from Docker in 2017: it focuses on running containers, pulling images, and managing network attachments, but does not build images or expose the developer-facing Docker CLI. It is smaller, faster, and more stable than Docker. CRI-O is Red Hat's alternative high-level runtime, created for OpenShift, with the same scope as containerd but with a different implementation. Both containerd and CRI-O implement the Kubernetes CRI (Container Runtime Interface), so Kubernetes can use either directly without Docker in the middle. Production clusters skip Docker because it adds overhead (another daemon, another layer of abstraction) without adding value when Kubernetes already provides the orchestration layer. Docker the company recognized this and donated containerd to CNCF in 2017; today containerd is the default runtime in EKS, GKE, AKS, and most self-managed clusters. Docker the developer tool remains popular for local development (`docker build`, `docker run`) but is rarely the production runtime. The split between developer experience (Docker) and production runtime (containerd) is now standard.

**Visual:**
```
Developer workflow:   docker build -> docker push -> registry
Production cluster:   kubelet -> containerd (or CRI-O) -> runc -> kernel

Docker daemon in production:  extra layer, extra overhead, no benefit
containerd / CRI-O:           smaller, faster, CRI-native, default in EKS/GKE/AKS

Docker remains popular for: local dev (docker build / docker run)
```

sections.body:
### Q1. Your Docker image is 1.5 GB and takes 8 minutes to build. How do you reduce both?
**Answer:** Image bloat and slow builds have well-known causes and cures. First, use multi-stage builds: a typical Dockerfile has a build stage with compilers and dev dependencies that produce a binary, and a runtime stage that copies only the binary into a minimal base image — the final image excludes the build toolchain. A Python image can drop from 1.2GB to 150MB by using a slim base (`python:3.11-slim` or `alpine`) and copying only the installed packages, not the build deps. Second, order Dockerfile instructions for cache efficiency: put rarely-changing layers (apt install, requirements.txt install) early, and frequently-changing layers (COPY source code) last, so a code change only invalidates the final layers. Third, use `.dockerignore` to exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, `__pycache__`, test fixtures, and other files that bloat the build context — Docker sends the entire context to the daemon before building. Fourth, combine `RUN` commands with `&&` to reduce the number of layers (each `RUN` is a layer). Fifth, use BuildKit (Docker 18.09+) which parallelizes independent build stages and skips unused stages. Sixth, choose a smaller base: `alpine` is 5MB, `distroless` is smaller and more secure, `ubuntu` is 80MB. Applying these typically takes a 1.5GB image to 100–200MB and an 8-minute build to 30–60 seconds. Spotify's 2016 migration to Docker documented exactly this playbook.

**Visual:**
```
Before: ubuntu:22.04 (80MB) + apt install (500MB) + npm install (700MB) + COPY src (50MB) = 1.3GB
        build 8 min (no cache hits)

After:  multi-stage:
          Stage 1 (builder): node:18 + npm install -> builds dist/
          Stage 2 (runtime): node:18-alpine + COPY --from=builder /dist -> 120MB
        .dockerignore excludes node_modules/.git/__pycache__
        RUN layers combined with && (fewer layers)
        BuildKit parallelizes, cache hits on early layers
        Result: 120MB image, 45s build
```

### Q2. Your Kubernetes pods keep getting OOMKilled. How do you diagnose and fix?
**Answer:** OOMKilled means the kernel killed a container process because it exceeded its cgroup memory limit, which in Kubernetes is `containers[].resources.limits.memory`. The diagnosis follows a structured path. First, confirm the OOMKilled state: `kubectl describe pod` shows `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled`. Second, distinguish limit-induced OOM from node-induced OOM: if the pod's limit is 512MB and it tried to allocate 600MB, the kernel OOM-killed it; if the node itself ran out of memory (system OOM), the kubelet evicted the pod — check `kubectl describe node` for memory pressure. Third, identify the memory consumer: it is usually the application (a memory leak, a large result set, an unbounded cache), the JVM (which often over-commits heap), or a sidecar (an agent with a leak). Pull a heap dump or memory profile before the OOM by raising the limit temporarily and triggering a dump at 80% usage. Fourth, fix the root cause: cap the application's memory (JVM `-Xmx`, Python `tracemalloc`, Node `--max-old-space-size`), fix the leak, add backpressure to prevent unbounded result sets, or tune the cache eviction policy. Fifth, right-size the limit: set `requests.memory` to typical usage and `limits.memory` to 1.5–2x that, giving headroom for spikes without over-provisioning. Sixth, alert on memory usage trends so you catch leaks before they OOM. Netflix's container team has a published playbook following exactly this pattern.

**Visual:**
```
1. Confirm:  kubectl describe pod -> Reason: OOMKilled
2. Source:   pod limit (kernel cgroup) vs node memory pressure (kubelet eviction)
3. Consumer: app (leak, big result, cache) / JVM heap / sidecar
4. Profile:  raise limit, dump at 80%, identify consumer
5. Fix:      cap app memory, fix leak, backpressure, cache eviction
6. Right-size: requests = typical, limits = 1.5-2x typical
7. Alert:    memory trend, catch leaks before OOM
```

### Q3. You need to run containers on a host that requires strong isolation for security-sensitive workloads. How do you architect it?
**Answer:** Standard Linux containers share the host kernel, which is insufficient isolation for security-sensitive workloads — a kernel exploit in one container can escape to the host and other containers. The architecture for stronger isolation layers additional boundaries. Option one, gVisor (Google): a userspace kernel that intercepts the container's syscalls and implements them in a sandboxed runtime, so the container never directly touches the host kernel. Stronger isolation, small performance penalty (5–15% on syscall-heavy workloads), used by Google App Engine and Cloud Run. Option two, Kata Containers: each container runs in a lightweight VM with its own kernel, giving VM-level isolation with container ergonomics. Strongest isolation, larger startup time (a few seconds), used by OpenStack and some AWS deployments. Option three, AWS Firecracker: a purpose-built microVM (used by Lambda and Fargate) with sub-125ms startup and full VM isolation — ideal for multi-tenant serverless. Option four, run containers inside EC2 instances with one tenant per instance: the simplest architecture, VM boundary provides isolation, container provides density and portability within the tenant. The right choice depends on threat model: for a single-tenant enterprise app, standard containers are fine. For a multi-tenant SaaS where one customer's container might be malicious, gVisor or Firecracker is appropriate. For regulatory workloads (payment processing, healthcare), Kata or per-tenant VMs are typical. AWS Lambda's use of Firecracker is the canonical reference for multi-tenant container security.

**Visual:**
```
Threat model         ->  Isolation choice
Single tenant app    ->  standard container (kernel shared)
Multi-tenant SaaS    ->  gVisor (userspace kernel) or Firecracker (microVM)
Regulated workload   ->  Kata Containers (VM per container) or per-tenant EC2

Trade-off:
  Standard:     0% overhead, weakest isolation
  gVisor:       5-15% overhead, strong
  Kata:         2-3s startup, strongest
  Firecracker:  <125ms startup, strong (Lambda/Fargate)
```

### Q4. You are migrating a stateful service from VMs to containers. What architectural decisions must you make?
**Answer:** Stateful services are harder to containerize than stateless ones because containers are designed to be ephemeral — when a container dies, its writable layer is discarded, and any data in it is lost. The decisions cascade from this. First, identify the state: where does the service write data that must survive container restart — local disk, in-memory cache, embedded database? Second, externalize the state to a persistent volume: Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) backed by EBS, EFS, or a networked storage system give the container a stable mount point that survives container restarts and can be re-attached to a replacement. Third, decide on the storage access mode: ReadWriteOnce (one pod at a time, suitable for databases) versus ReadWriteMany (multiple pods, suitable for shared file storage) — the choice constrains the storage backend. Fourth, use a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment: StatefulSets give pods stable identities (pod-0, pod-1, pod-2), stable network names, and ordered startup/shutdown, which are essential for clustered databases like Cassandra, Kafka, or etcd. Fifth, handle leader election and failover explicitly: a stateful service typically has a primary and replicas, and failover logic must be aware of the StatefulSet identity. Sixth, plan backups separately — container orchestration does not handle database backups; you need a sidecar or external job. Seventh, consider whether containerization is even the right choice: for many stateful workloads, managed services (RDS, ElastiCache, MSK) are simpler and more reliable than self-operating in containers. Netflix's Cassandra deployment runs in containers via their internal Titus platform, but most companies are better served by Amazon Keyspaces or a managed equivalent.

**Visual:**
```
Stateful containerization:
1. Identify state (local disk, in-memory, embedded DB)
2. Externalize -> PersistentVolumeClaim (EBS/EFS backing)
3. Access mode: RWO (one pod) vs RWX (shared)
4. Use StatefulSet (stable identity, ordered startup)
5. Leader election + failover logic
6. Backups via sidecar or external job (orchestrator does not do this)
7. Question: managed service (RDS/MSK) is simpler - is containerization justified?
```

### Q5. Your team's Kubernetes cluster is hard to operate and developers complain about YAML fatigue. How do you improve the developer experience?
**Answer:** Kubernetes YAML fatigue is a real and well-documented problem — developers writing raw Deployments, Services, Ingresses, ConfigMaps, and Secrets for every service ends up being hundreds of lines of boilerplate per app, with subtle errors that fail at deploy time. The improvements layer three categories of tooling. First, templating and packaging: Helm charts let you parameterize manifests and reuse them across services — one Helm chart can deploy 100 microservices with per-service values. Kustomize is the alternative for overlay-based customization without templating. Second, higher-level abstractions: define internal CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions) that express concepts closer to the application — an `App` CRD with fields for image, replicas, and ingress, with a controller that expands it into Deployments, Services, and Ingresses. This is what Backstage, OAM, and most internal platforms do. Third, a developer portal: a UI like Backstage where developers fill in a form, click "deploy," and the platform generates and applies the manifests. The portal also provides visibility (logs, metrics, deploy history) so developers do not need `kubectl` access. Fourth, golden path templates: pre-built Helm charts for the common service types (web service, background worker, scheduled job) that include observability, secrets, and ingress by default. Fifth, GitOps deployment: developers push code, CI builds an image, Argo CD or Flux detects the new image and updates the cluster — developers never touch manifests directly. Spotify's Backstage and Netflix's internal platform are the canonical references. The goal is that a developer can deploy a new service in 5 minutes without writing a single line of YAML.

**Visual:**
```
Before:  developer writes Deployment + Service + Ingress + ConfigMap + Secret
         = 200 lines of YAML per service, errors at deploy time

After:   developer fills form in Backstage portal
           -> generates Helm chart from golden-path template
           -> commits to git
           -> Argo CD detects change, applies to cluster
         developer writes 0 lines of YAML, deploy in 5 minutes
```

### Q6. A container image works on your Mac but fails on the production Linux cluster with "exec format error." What is happening?
**Answer:** "Exec format error" on a Linux cluster for an image that ran on a Mac is almost always a CPU architecture mismatch. Macs since 2020 ship with Apple Silicon (ARM64), so `docker build` on a Mac produces an ARM64 image by default. The production cluster runs on x86_64 (Intel/AMD) EC2 or GCE instances, which cannot execute ARM64 binaries — hence the kernel's exec format error when it tries to run the binary. The fix is multi-architecture image builds. Docker BuildKit (default since Docker 23) supports `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` which uses QEMU emulation or remote builders to produce a manifest list that points to per-architecture images; the cluster pulls the right variant automatically. For performance, use native ARM and x86 builders (GitHub Actions has both, AWS Graviton for ARM, standard EC2 for x86) rather than QEMU emulation, which is 5–10x slower. The other common cause of exec format error is a binary built for a different OS (Windows binary on Linux, or vice versa), but that is rarer with containers because the base image enforces OS compatibility. The growing prevalence of ARM clouds (AWS Graviton, GCP Tau, Azure Cobalt) makes multi-arch builds a default practice in 2024 — single-arch images are a deployment footgun. Netflix's migration of streaming workloads to Graviton in 2022 documented exactly this build pipeline change.

**Visual:**
```
Mac (Apple Silicon)         Production cluster (EC2 x86_64)
  docker build              docker pull
  -> ARM64 image            -> tries to exec ARM64 binary on x86
                             -> "exec format error"

Fix:  docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64
       -> manifest list with per-arch images
       -> cluster pulls matching arch automatically

Best:  CI uses native ARM builder (Graviton) + native x86 builder
       -> faster than QEMU emulation, correct arch for each env
```

### Q7. You are designing a container platform for a multi-tenant SaaS where customers can submit arbitrary code (like a function-as-a-service). How do you architect isolation?
**Answer:** Arbitrary customer code is the highest-risk workload because the code may be malicious — it may try to escape the container, mine cryptocurrency, attack other tenants, or consume all host resources. The architecture must layer multiple isolation boundaries. First, never use standard Linux containers for untrusted code — kernel escapes are real (CVE-2019-5736, CVE-2022-0185) and a single escape compromises every tenant on the host. Second, use a VM-isolated runtime: AWS Firecracker (open-sourced 2018) is purpose-built for this — a microVM with sub-125ms startup, full kernel isolation, used by Lambda, Fargate, and Fly.io. Google gVisor is an alternative that intercepts syscalls in userspace. Kata Containers is another, using nested KVM. Third, give each workload a dedicated kernel — this is the fundamental difference from standard containers, and it is non-negotiable for multi-tenant untrusted code. Fourth, enforce strict resource limits: CPU, memory, disk, and network quotas per workload via cgroups, with hard caps to prevent noisy-neighbor and crypto-mining attacks. Fifth, network isolation: each workload runs in its own network namespace with no inbound access and tightly restricted outbound (egress allowlist to specific APIs). Sixth, ephemeral storage: the writable layer is discarded after the workload exits, and any persistent state goes through a vetted API. Seventh, observability and abuse detection: log every workload invocation, monitor for crypto-mining signatures, rate-limit per tenant. AWS Lambda, Cloud Run, and Fly.io all follow this architecture, and the security model has been validated by years of public multi-tenant operation without a confirmed escape.

**Visual:**
```
Layered isolation for untrusted code:
1. No standard containers (kernel escape risk)
2. Firecracker microVM per workload (dedicated kernel, <125ms startup)
   OR gVisor (userspace syscall interception)
   OR Kata (nested KVM)
3. Hard cgroup limits (cpu, mem, disk, net) - prevents noisy-neighbor
4. Network namespace: no inbound, egress allowlist only
5. Ephemeral storage: writable layer discarded after exit
6. Observability: log every run, detect crypto-mining signatures
7. Rate-limit per tenant, abuse detection pipeline

Validated by: AWS Lambda, Cloud Run, Fly.io - years of public multi-tenant
```

quiz.explanation: A single container is trivial — docker run and you are done. A production fleet of thousands of containers across hundreds of hosts is intractable without an orchestrator.
